Abstract:

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, algorithmic governance, and digital infrastructures has transformed the conditions under which human cognition and memory are constituted. A conventional understanding of memory as an internal cognitive faculty has become inadequate, as remembering today emerges through interactions among biological, technological, and material systems. In this context, posthumanism, a framework that challenges anthropocentric subjectivity by recognising human existence as relational and entangled with technological and nonhuman agencies, has emerged as a lens for reconceiving memory beyond the bounded, autonomous subject. While posthumanist theory has extensively interrogated technological and nonhuman agency, and memory studies has separately registered the growing entanglement of remembrance with digital systems, the two fields have rarely been brought into sustained critical dialogue, a gap that has not fully theorised memory as simultaneously distributed and remembered, cognitively extended and narratively experienced. Graphic narratives offer a formal structure peculiarly suited to addressing this gap. As a hybrid literary form that combines sequential images, text, and page design, graphic narratives construct meaning through the interplay and disjunction of textual and visual registers. However, despite the emerging body of scholarship on graphic narratives as a novel modality, their capacity to visually materialise fragmented, distributed, and technologically mediated forms of remembrance remains critically overlooked. This study examines how graphic novel&rsquos formal apparatus materially enacts the fragmented and distributed structures of posthuman memory by closely reading the textual and visual registers of contemporary science fiction graphic novels Square Eyes (2018), Gregory Suicide (2017), Upgrade Soul (2018), and Carbon &amp Silicon (2021), each foregrounding a distinct modality of posthuman memory. Drawing on a theoretical framework that combines posthumanism, memory studies, and comics theory, this study positions the select texts as productive sites for investigating memory&rsquos changing modalities as they become perceptible under posthuman conditions in which the act of remembrance is no longer bound to the individual, biological subject but distributed across human, technological, material, and ecological relations.

Keywords: Posthumanism, Memory Studies, Graphic Novels, Science Fiction, Relationality, Materiality
